opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core issue is that the physical world is fundamentally continuous, and transformers, as powerful as they are, were built around discrete tokens. Language is naturally tokenized, so that fit is great. But when you're modeling fluid flow, weather, plasma in a fusion reactor, or the stresses in a material, the underlying reality is governed by partial differential equations over continuous fields. If you chop that into a fixed grid of patches and treat it like a sequence of tokens, you're baking in a particular resolution, and the model learns something tied to that discretization rather than the actual physics.

That's what motivated our work on neural operators. Instead of learning a mapping between finite-dimensional vectors, you learn a mapping between function spaces. So the model is resolution-invariant, or discretization-agnostic: you can train on coarse data, query it at a finer resolution, and it still gives you sensible answers, sometimes even zero-shot super-resolution. That matters enormously in science, because data comes from very different sources, from simulations at different fidelities, sensors on irregular meshes, and experimental measurements, and you want one model that can absorb all of it.

The second issue is efficiency and structure. Physics has multiscale phenomena: turbulence is a classic example where energy cascades across scales. Operations like the Fourier neural operator let you capture global interactions efficiently in the spectral domain, rather than paying the quadratic cost of attention over a huge number of grid points. And you can incorporate physical constraints directly, through physics-informed losses or conservation laws, so the model doesn't just fit the data but actually respects the governing equations. That's crucial when you want to extrapolate or trust the model in safety-critical settings.

Now, I don't think it's transformers versus everything else. Attention is a very useful component, and you can actually formulate attention as a kind of integral operator, so there's a nice unification there. The point is that the architecture needs to respect the nature of the domain. For language, discrete tokens. For the physical world, continuous functions, multiple scales, and physical laws. And we've seen the payoff: models like FourCastNet doing weather forecasting tens of thousands of times faster than traditional numerical methods, with competitive accuracy. That's the kind of leap you get when the architecture matches the physics.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that transformers were built for language, and language is discrete. You have a finite vocabulary, tokens at fixed positions, and you can get away with treating everything as a sequence. The physical world isn't like that. Physics lives in continuous space and time. When you model fluid flow, weather, or stress in a material, the underlying object is a function defined everywhere in a domain, not a list of tokens. The grid you happen to sample on is an artifact of your sensors or your simulator, not a property of the physics.

So if you take a transformer and feed it a 100-by-100 grid of pressure values, it learns something tied to that exact grid. Change the resolution, change the mesh, and the model falls apart. That's the first problem: there's no notion of resolution invariance. What we really want is to learn the operator, the mapping from one function to another, so that the same model works at any discretization. That's the idea behind neural operators. The Fourier neural operator, for instance, does its heavy lifting in frequency space, where a convolution becomes a multiplication and you naturally get a global, mesh-independent representation. You can train at low resolution and evaluate at higher resolution, and it actually works, which transformers don't give you for free.

The second problem is cost. Attention scales quadratically in the number of tokens. A 3D simulation at any reasonable resolution has millions of points. You can patch things up, you can use sparse attention, but you're fighting the architecture instead of working with it. Operations in Fourier space scale closer to N log N and handle long-range interactions directly, which matters because in physics a disturbance on one side of the domain affects the other side.

The third piece is inductive bias. Physical systems obey conservation laws, symmetries, PDE constraints. A general-purpose sequence model knows none of that and has to rediscover it from data, which means you need enormous amounts of data and still get solutions that violate the physics. With operator learning you can bake constraints in, or add physics-informed losses, and the model generalizes with far fewer examples.

None of this means attention is useless. We use attention within neural operator frameworks when it fits, for example for irregular geometries. But as the backbone for modeling the continuous world, you want something that respects continuity, resolution, and physical structure. We've seen this pay off in weather forecasting, in carbon capture modeling, in plasma control for fusion, where neural operators give you tens of thousands of times speedup over numerical solvers while generalizing across scales. That's the regime where the right architecture isn't a nice-to-have, it's what makes the problem solvable at all.

astra-6.text:
Transformers have been very successful at learning patterns in sequences, but the physical world isn’t naturally a sequence of tokens. It involves continuous fields—velocity, pressure, temperature—evolving over space and time. And those dynamics have structure: conservation laws, symmetries, and interactions across many scales.

A transformer can certainly learn aspects of that. The question is whether it’s the most efficient architecture, and whether it generalizes when you change the resolution, the geometry, or the conditions. Fitting trajectories in your training data is different from learning dynamics that remain accurate in a new setting.

That’s why I’m excited about neural operators. Instead of learning a mapping between fixed-size vectors, you learn a mapping between functions—for example, from an initial velocity field to a future velocity field. That gives you a natural way to work across discretizations, rather than tying the model to one particular grid.

So I don’t see this as simply replacing transformers. It’s about building architectures with the right structure for the problem, and combining learning with physics. We want models that are fast, but also reliable enough to support scientific discovery and engineering design.

sol-6.1.text:
Transformers have been very successful at modeling language, but the physical world presents a different set of challenges. You have continuous fields evolving in space and time, interactions across many scales, and constraints such as conservation laws. We need architectures that can capture that structure and generalize when the resolution or the conditions change.

For example, with neural operators, the goal is to learn a mapping between functions—say, from an initial fluid state to its future evolution—rather than learn a mapping tied to one fixed grid. That gives us a way to work across resolutions and build in useful structure from the underlying physics.

I don’t think this means attention has no role. It means we should choose the architecture based on the problem. Predicting something that looks plausible is one thing; accurately predicting a physical system over time is a much stronger requirement.
